flashcards.front: Definitions and Scope of Economics — Focus
flashcards.back: Production, accumulation and distribution of wealth. Smith is called the Father of Economics.

flashcards.front: Definitions and Scope of Economics — Other supporters
flashcards.back: J.B. Say, J.S. Mill, Walker.

flashcards.front: Definitions and Scope of Economics — Features
flashcards.back: Studies ordinary people; studies material welfare only; economics is a social science; wealth is a means, not an end.
Consumption, production, exchange (trade), distribution (rent, wages, interest, profit) and public finance.
Study of individual units vs the whole economy.
What is vs what ought to be.
Poverty, unemployment, inflation, inequality, regional imbalance, population growth.
Exchange rates, balance of payments, WTO, globalisation.
Deals with "what is", "what was", "what will be". Based on facts, can be tested and verified with data. Free from value judgements.
Deals with "what ought to be". Based on opinions, ethics and value judgements. Cannot be proved true or false by data alone.
Policy (normative) needs analysis of facts (positive).

Has laws (law of demand, law of diminishing returns), uses scientific method (observation, hypothesis, testing, conclusion), but laws are tendencies, not exact like physical sciences, because human behaviour varies.
Deductive (general to particular — logic, assumptions), inductive (particular to general — data, observation).
Micro = small, macro = large.
Study of individual economic units — a consumer, household, firm, industry, a single market.

flashcards.front: Also called price theory. Main tool
flashcards.back: Marginal analysis. Method: partial equilibrium analysis (one market at a time).
General equilibrium analysis.

flashcards.front: Paradox of thrift and fallacy of composition show the two are linked
flashcards.back: What is true for the individual need not be true for the whole.
Ignores whole-economy interlinkages; limitations of macro: ignores individual differences and structure.
Scarcity of resources + unlimited wants + alternative uses of resources = problem of choice.
Land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship.

flashcards.front: Fundamental Problems of an Economy — Optimum Allocation o... — How to produce? — choice of technique
flashcards.back: Labour-intensive vs capital-intensive; large scale vs small scale. Decided by relative factor prices and efficiency (least-cost combination).
Solved by price mechanism; private ownership; profit motive; consumer sovereignty (e.g. USA).
Solved by central planning authority; state ownership (e.g. erstwhile USSR, China earlier).
Both private and public sectors co-exist; market plus government regulation (e.g. India, UK, France).
Economic growth — more resources, better technology, education, capital accumulation.
Loss of resources — war, natural disasters, population decline.
Technology improves in only one good — only that axis intercept changes.
Constant opportunity cost (resources perfectly substitutable). Convex PPC: decreasing opportunity cost (rare).
Illustrates scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, unemployment, growth, and the central problems of what to produce.
Movement along the PPC = reallocating resources between goods; shift of PPC = change in productive capacity.
Form utility, place utility, time utility, service utility, possession utility.
Utility can be measured in numbers called utils. Basis of marginal utility analysis.
The sum of utilities obtained from consuming all units of a commodity. TU = ΣMU.
The addition to total utility from consuming one more unit. MU = ΔTU/ΔQ, or MUn = TUn − TUn−1.

flashcards.front: Definition of Utility and Marginal Utility — Explanation
flashcards.back: The first unit satisfies the most urgent want; later units satisfy less intense wants.

flashcards.front: Definition of Utility and Marginal Utility — Applications
flashcards.back: Consumption, production (factor allocation), public finance, saving vs spending.
A set of indifference curves; higher IC = higher satisfaction.
Rationality; ordinal utility; non-satiation (more is better); diminishing MRS; transitivity/consistency of preferences; given tastes and income.
Shows all combinations of two goods a consumer can buy with a given income and given prices. Equation: M = Px·X + Py·Y.
X-axis = M/Px; Y-axis = M/Py. Slope = −Px/Py (price ratio).

flashcards.front: Indifference Curve and Budget Constraint — Example
flashcards.back: Income Rs. 100, Px = Rs. 10, Py = Rs. 20 — maximum X = 10, maximum Y = 5.
Affordable and exhaust income; inside: affordable but income left; outside: unaffordable.
The consumer is in equilibrium where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve.
Slope of IC = slope of budget line, i.e. MRSxy = Px/Py (equivalent to MUx/MUy = Px/Py, giving MUx/Px = MUy/Py).
IC must be convex to the origin at the point of tangency (MRS is diminishing).
Locus of equilibrium points as the price of one good changes. Used to derive the demand curve.
Change in consumption because of change in relative price, keeping real income constant — always negative.
Change in consumption due to change in real income — positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods.
Qd = f(Px, Pr, Y, T, E, N, …) — i.e. demand depends on own price, price of related goods, income, tastes, expectations, population.
Inverse relation (law of demand).
Substitutes (tea–coffee): price of one rises, demand for the other rises. Complements (car–petrol): price of one rises, demand for the other falls.
A table showing quantity demanded at different prices. Individual demand schedule for one consumer; market demand schedule is a horizontal sum.
Graphical representation of the demand schedule — price on Y axis, quantity on X axis; slopes downward from left to right.
Horizontal summation of all individual demand curves at each price.

Other things remaining the same (ceteris paribus), when the price of a commodity falls, its quantity demanded rises, and when price rises, quantity demanded falls — an inverse relationship between price and quantity. (Marshall.)

flashcards.front: Law of Demand and Exceptions — Assumptions
flashcards.back: No change in consumer's income; no change in tastes and fashion; no change in prices of related goods; no expectation of future price change; no change in population; no change in government policy; normal commodity.

flashcards.front: Speculative markets — shares, gold, real estate
flashcards.back: Rising prices attract more buyers.
Normally downward sloping (negative slope); upward sloping for exceptions.
Price falls, quantity demanded rises — downward movement.
Price rises, quantity demanded falls — upward movement.
Rightward shift — more is demanded at each price.
Leftward shift — less is demanded at each price.

flashcards.front: Causes of an increase in demand
flashcards.back: Rise in income (normal goods); rise in price of substitutes; fall in price of complements; favourable change in taste; expectation of price rise; growth in population; advertising.
Percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.

flashcards.front: Elasticity of Demand and its Applications — Percentage (proportionate) method
flashcards.back: Ed = % change in Q ÷ % change in P.

flashcards.front: Price falls from Rs. 10 to Rs. 8 and quantity rises from 100 to 120
flashcards.back: %ΔQ = 20%, %ΔP = −20%, so Ed = 1 (unitary).

flashcards.front: Price rises from Rs. 20 to Rs. 25; demand falls from 80 to 60
Price falls from Rs. 5 to Rs. 4; quantity rises from 50 to 80
flashcards.back: %ΔQ = 60%, %ΔP = 20%, Ed = 3 (elastic).

flashcards.front: Government — tax policy (tax goods with inelastic demand
flashcards.back: Petrol, tobacco, liquor for revenue); subsidies; minimum support prices.
Direct relation — higher price, higher supply.

flashcards.front: Supply — Cost of production / prices of factor inputs
flashcards.back: Higher costs reduce supply (supply curve shifts left).
Improved technology lowers cost and increases supply.
Taxes reduce supply; subsidies increase supply.

flashcards.front: Supply — Number of firms in the industry
flashcards.back: More firms mean more market supply.
Profit maximisation vs sales maximisation.

Other things remaining constant, as the price of a commodity rises, its quantity supplied rises, and as price falls, quantity supplied falls — a direct (positive) relationship between price and quantity supplied.

flashcards.front: Law of Supply and Deriving the Supply Curve — Assumptions
flashcards.back: Cost of production constant; technology constant; no change in government policy; prices of related goods constant; no change in number of sellers; no expectations of price change; no change in natural conditions.
Upward sloping from left to right. Individual supply curve — one firm; market supply curve is the horizontal sum of all individual supply curves.

From the supply schedule by plotting price (Y) vs quantity supplied (X). In perfect competition, the firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of its MC curve above the AVC minimum (shutdown point).

Caused only by a change in the price of the good; shown by movement along the same supply curve. Expansion of supply (price rises, supply rises — upward movement); contraction of supply (price falls — downward movement).

Caused by changes in non-price factors; shown by shift of the whole supply curve. Increase in supply — rightward shift (technology improves, input prices fall, subsidy, more firms). Decrease in supply — leftward shift (higher input costs, taxes, bad weather, fewer firms).
At a price above equilibrium, Qs > Qd — competition among sellers pushes price down.
At a price below equilibrium, Qd > Qs — competition among buyers pushes price up.
Forces automatically restore the equilibrium after a disturbance. Unstable equilibrium: forces push away from equilibrium.
If demand and supply increase by the same proportion, price remains unchanged and quantity rises.

Price ceiling (maximum price below equilibrium, e.g. rent control, essential commodities) creates shortage and black markets. Price floor (minimum price above equilibrium, e.g. Minimum Support Price, minimum wage) creates surplus.
If Qd = 100 − 5P and Qs = 20 + 3P, equilibrium: 100 − 5P = 20 + 3P, so 8P = 80, P = 10, Q = 50.
Degree of responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price. Es = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q). It is positive due to direct relation.

flashcards.front: Geometric rule for a straight-line supply curve
flashcards.back: If it passes through the origin Es = 1; if it cuts the Y-axis, Es > 1; if it cuts the X-axis, Es < 1 (regardless of slope).
Percentage method, point method, arc method.

flashcards.front: Price rises from Rs. 10 to Rs. 12; supply rises from 100 to 130
flashcards.back: %ΔQ = 30%, %ΔP = 20%, Es = 1.5 (elastic).

flashcards.front: Price rises from Rs. 20 to Rs. 22; supply rises from 50 to 52
flashcards.back: %ΔQ = 4%, %ΔP = 10%, Es = 0.4 (inelastic).

flashcards.front: Elasticity of Supply and its Application — Applications
flashcards.back: Decides tax incidence (more of tax is borne by sellers with inelastic supply); helps in agricultural pricing and MSP; guides government on price stabilisation; helps firms in capacity planning; explains price volatility in agricultural markets (inelastic supply causes big price swings);

The process of creating or adding utility (value) to goods and services — transforming inputs into outputs. Production does not mean creation of matter; it means creation of utility (form, place, time, service utility).

flashcards.front: Meaning and Definition of Production — Land
flashcards.back: All natural resources — soil, minerals, forests, water, climate. Features: gift of nature; fixed in supply (perfectly inelastic in total); passive factor; heterogeneous in fertility and location; immobile geographically. Reward: rent.

flashcards.front: Meaning and Definition of Production — Labour
flashcards.back: Physical and mental human effort for a reward. Features: perishable; inseparable from labourer; active; varies in efficiency; weak bargaining power; supply is affected by population and wage rate. Reward: wages.

flashcards.front: Meaning and Definition of Production — Entrepreneur / Organisation
flashcards.back: Coordinates other factors, takes decisions and bears risk and uncertainty. Functions: initiative, risk-bearing, innovation (Schumpeter), management, decision making. Reward: profit.
Fixed vs circulating; physical vs human; private vs social.
Splitting of production into small tasks — raises efficiency; limits: size of the market.

The technical relationship between physical inputs and the maximum output that can be produced with a given state of technology. Q = f(L, K, N, O …), where Q = output; L = labour; K = capital; N = land; O = organisation.

flashcards.front: Production Function — One Variable and Two Variable Inputs — Features
flashcards.back: Relates to a given period; assumes a given technology (change in technology shifts the function); shows the maximum output from given inputs (efficiency); inputs must be used in efficient combinations; defined for a specific product.

flashcards.front: Production function with one variable input (short run)
flashcards.back: Q = f(L), with K fixed. Studied through Total Product (TP), Average Product (AP) and Marginal Product (MP).

flashcards.front: Production function with two variable inputs (long run)
flashcards.back: Q = f(L, K), studied through isoquants and returns to scale.
Q = A·Lα·Kβ — α and β are output elasticities of labour and capital. If α + β = 1, constant returns to scale; >1 increasing; <1 decreasing. Suited to two-factor analysis.
Inputs used in fixed ratios (L-shaped isoquants).

flashcards.front: Short-Run Production Function — Law of Variable Proportion — Assumptions
flashcards.back: Technology constant; at least one factor is fixed; variable factors are homogeneous; the possibility of varying factor proportions exists; short-run phenomenon.
From origin to the point where AP is maximum (MP = AP). Not a rational stage to stop — fixed factors underutilised.
From maximum AP to the point where MP = 0 (TP maximum). The rational stage of production — the firm operates here.
MP < 0, TP falls. A rational producer never operates here.

Better utilisation of fixed factors; division of labour and specialisation. Causes of diminishing returns: overuse of fixed factor; imperfect substitutability of factors; poor coordination. Causes of negative returns: overcrowding and managerial inefficiency.
Originally for agriculture (Ricardo, Malthus); applies to all production activities. Delayed by better technology, but not avoided.
How output changes when all inputs are changed in the same proportion (the scale changes), in the long run.

Output rises by a larger proportion than inputs (inputs double, output more than doubles). Causes: division of labour, indivisibility of factors, technical economies, managerial economies, marketing economies.
Output rises in the same proportion (inputs double, output doubles). Typical when internal economies and diseconomies offset each other. Cobb–Douglas with α + β = 1.
Output rises by a smaller proportion (inputs double, output less than doubles). Causes: managerial diseconomies, coordination problems, labour disputes, exhaustion of natural resources.
IRS first, then CRS over a range, then DRS.
A curve showing all possible combinations of two inputs (labour and capital) that yield the same level of output.
Set of isoquants; a higher isoquant means higher output.
The rate at which one input can be substituted for another without changing output; MRTS = −ΔK/ΔL = MPL/MPK. Diminishes along an isoquant.
Slopes downward; convex to the origin (diminishing MRTS); two isoquants never intersect; higher isoquant means more output; do not touch the axes; not necessarily parallel.
Isoquants measure physical output (cardinal, can be labelled 100, 200); ICs measure satisfaction (ordinal). Both are convex and non-intersecting.

flashcards.front: Marginal rate of substitution vs MRTS
flashcards.back: MRS relates to consumers (utility); MRTS relates to producers (output).
Total expenditure in money terms. Real cost: effort and sacrifice of the factor owners (Marshall: pains of labour, abstinence of capital).
Value of the next best alternative forgone.
Constant at all outputs. TVC: rises with output. TC = TFC + TVC.
All costs are variable; no fixed cost.
Derived from short-run marginal costs; cuts LAC at its minimum; flatter than SMC.
Lowest output at which LAC is minimised.
Reduction in average cost as output expands (scale of production rises).

Large machines, specialisation, indivisibility. Managerial: specialised managers. Marketing: bulk advertising and distribution. Financial: cheaper credit. Risk-bearing: diversification. Labour: division of labour. Purchasing: bulk discounts.
Rise in AC when the firm becomes too large — management coordination problems, labour disputes, red tape, scarce inputs. External diseconomies: congestion, pollution, rising input prices.

Reduction in average cost when a firm produces a variety of related products together rather than separately (shared inputs: equipment, brand, distribution, R&D) — e.g. a dairy producing milk, curd and butter; a bank offering several services.
Scale — about the volume of one product; scope — about the variety of products.
Price is constant; AR = MR = P (horizontal line); TR is a straight line from the origin.
MR = AR × (e − 1)/e, and e = AR/(AR − MR).
TR − TC > 0 beyond normal profit (AR > AC).
TR = TC (AR = AC; zero economic profit).
Profit is maximum where the vertical gap between TR and TC is greatest.
Sales maximisation (Baumol), managerial utility (Williamson), satisficing (Simon), growth.
Shows all combinations of two inputs (labour and capital) that a firm can buy with a given total cost (outlay) and given factor prices. TC = w·L + r·K (w = wage rate, r = rental rate of capital).
TC/w on the labour axis; TC/r on the capital axis. Slope = −w/r (ratio of factor prices).
Increase in outlay — parallel outward shift; decrease — inward; change in w — rotates around the capital-axis intercept; change in r — rotates around the labour-axis intercept.
Isocost is to the producer what the budget line is to the consumer.
MRTSLK = w/r (slope of isoquant = slope of isocost), which is MPL/MPK = w/r, or MPL/w = MPK/r.
Isoquant must be convex to the origin at the equilibrium point.

flashcards.front: Maximising output subject to a cost constraint
flashcards.back: Reach the highest isoquant within the given isocost line.

flashcards.front: Minimising cost for a given output
flashcards.back: Reach the lowest isocost line touching the given isoquant.

flashcards.front: Effect of change in factor prices
flashcards.back: If wages rise relative to the price of capital, the firm substitutes capital for labour (new tangency on a steeper isocost line).

flashcards.front: Difference between consumer's and producer's equilibrium
flashcards.back: Consumer maximises satisfaction (ordinal); producer maximises output (cardinal).
In economics, any arrangement (place, physical or virtual) in which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods and services at a price. It need not be a specific place.
A commodity; buyers and sellers; contact between them; a price; competition.

flashcards.front: Meaning and Definition of Market — By area
flashcards.back: Local, regional, national, international.

flashcards.front: Meaning and Definition of Market — By time (Marshall)
flashcards.back: Very short period (market period), short period, long period, very long period (secular).

flashcards.front: Meaning and Definition of Market — By competition (most important)
flashcards.back: Perfect competition and imperfect competition (monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, duopoly; also monopsony, oligopsony).
Number of buyers and sellers, nature of the product (homogeneous/differentiated), freedom of entry and exit, knowledge of market, mobility of factors, and control over price.
By interaction of industry demand and industry supply. The firm accepts that price.

Condition MR = MC, with MC cutting MR from below. Three outcomes: supernormal profit (P > AC), normal profit (P = AC) and loss (P < AC but ≥ AVC). Shutdown if P < AVC. Firm's short-run supply curve = MC above minimum AVC.

Free entry and exit make firms earn only normal profit: P = MR = SMC = SAC = LMC = LAC (minimum LAC). Firm produces at the optimum scale — maximum productive and allocative efficiency (P = MC). If supernormal profits exist, new firms enter and price falls; if losses, firms exit and price rises.

Efficient allocation; consumer sovereignty; no exploitation; lowest price; optimum output. Demerits: unrealistic; no innovation or product variety; no economies of scale benefit beyond a limit; no advertising information.
Any market where one or more of the conditions of perfect competition is not fulfilled — sellers have some control over price. Includes monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly.
A market with a single seller of a product having no close substitutes, with barriers to entry.
Price control, anti-trust law (Competition Act 2002 in India — CCI), nationalisation, taxation.
Many sellers selling differentiated but closely related (substitute) products.
Market with a few large sellers, each aware of rivals' reactions.
Two firms, each assumes the rival's output is fixed. Bertrand model: firms compete on price.
Monopsony (single buyer), oligopsony (few buyers), bilateral monopoly (single seller meets single buyer).
